operationalization: Classify incubated double-yolked fowl eggs by whether a membrane separates the yolks, then score each hatchling or late embryo for body, head, leg and wing number. Separated yolks yielding two ordinary chicks, and continuous yolks yielding one body and head with four legs and four wings, would support the claim; the reverse pattern, or ordinary single chicks from continuous yolks, would refute it.
obstacles: Hatchery and embryology reports describe double-yolk monsters, but no open dataset pairs yolk continuity with chick morphology.
Published cases are biased toward conspicuous deformities.
rationale: The morphological contrast is straightforward to score in the domestic fowl. What exists is a scatter of poultry case reports, which can illustrate the phenomenon and cannot estimate how regularly fused yolks produce the four-limbed form. A decisive test needs a series that records membrane status and the resulting anatomy together.

operationalization: Count births with both male and female external genitalia, or an equivalent disorder of sex development, per live birth in humans and in goats, and compare those rates with other livestock. Occurrence in both species, with a higher rate in goats, would support the claim; absence from either species, or a higher rate in another familiar mammal, would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: OMIA: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: catalogued polled intersex syndrome and other disorders of sexual development in goats and other domestic mammals

candidate_datasets.name: EUROCAT
candidate_datasets.role: population prevalence of human congenital anomalies, including indeterminate sex and related genital malformations

candidate_datasets.name: Orphanet
candidate_datasets.role: inventory of human disorders of sex development against which the goat syndrome can be compared

obstacles: Goat polled intersex syndrome is an XX sex-reversal spectrum, broader than simultaneous male and female external organs.
Farm ascertainment and clinical registries use different denominators, so 'especially in goats' is only roughly comparable.
rationale: Both the human and the goat phenomena are recorded in public catalogues, and the goat syndrome is common enough in polled herds to test the 'especially' clause against humans. The catalogues are genetic and clinical inventories rather than matched birth-rate tables, and most wild mammals are missing. A rate comparison is feasible for humans, goats and a few other domestic species, and it leaves the wider animal kingdom open.

operationalization: In population congenital-anomaly registries, compare the prevalence of absent heart and of total liver agenesis with asplenia, polysplenia and unilateral renal agenesis among births and stillbirths. Heart or complete liver absence among births that meet the registry's inclusion rules would refute the corresponding universal; asplenia and single-kidney cases with intact heart and liver would support the contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: EUROCAT
candidate_datasets.role: European birth-population rates of cardiac, hepatic, splenic and renal congenital anomalies

obstacles: The claim covers all animals with blood, while open registries are essentially human.
Acardiac twins and very early lethal defects sit awkwardly against 'born without a heart'.
rationale: EUROCAT publishes prevalence for the organ absences the claim contrasts, so the human case can be tested directly. A single qualifying birth without a heart or without any liver tissue would refute the universal, and asplenia and renal agenesis are common enough to test the positive contrast. Wild vertebrates and most domestic species are outside that registry, so the full scope stays out of reach.

operationalization: Regress litter size, clutch size or fecundity on adult body mass separately for mammals, birds and fishes, with a phylogenetic control. A negative slope within each locomotor group would support the claim; a flat or positive slope in any of those groups would refute it for that group.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and litter or clutch size for mammals, birds and other vertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: harmonised body mass and litter or clutch size for more than 20,000 birds, mammals and reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: body length and fecundity for the swimming animals in the claim

obstacles: Body mass, phylogeny and offspring number are entangled, so the slope should be estimated with a phylogenetic regression.
The nutriment explanation is an interpretation of that slope, which the same tables do not measure directly.
rationale: Offspring number and adult size are standard columns in open life-history databases covering the walking, flying and swimming groups named in the claim. A phylogenetic regression is ordinary comparative biology and can be run in days. The size pattern itself is decidable from these tables; the further claim that nutriment is diverted into bodily growth is only as strong as the partial correlation.

operationalization: Tabulate human births and neonatal deaths by week of gestation from about 28 to 44 weeks, and compare the width of that viable span with published gestation ranges for other mammals. Survival that rises steadily with gestational age would refute a special disadvantage of eight-month births; a uniquely wide human distribution would be required to support the 'man alone' clause.

candidate_datasets.name: NBER Vital Statistics Natality Birth Data
candidate_datasets.role: US birth microdata with obstetric gestational age, for the span from seven to ten months

candidate_datasets.name: Euro-Peristat
candidate_datasets.role: European births and perinatal mortality by gestational-age group

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: typical gestation lengths for other mammals, as a comparison with the human range

obstacles: Ancient months may be lunar, so seven, eight and ten months need a pre-set day count before the survival curve is read.
AnAge stores a typical gestation, so within-species irregularity in other animals is only partly visible.
rationale: Open birth files and European perinatal indicators give human survival by gestational age at the resolution needed to test whether eight-month infants fare worse than seven-month infants. Comparative databases give a single gestation length for most other species, which can show that many mammals are not fixed to the day and cannot show that humans alone are irregular. The survival clause is decidable now; the uniqueness clause is only partly covered.

operationalization: For a phylogenetic sample of mammals, record whether females copulate or show sexual receptivity during a confirmed pregnancy. Receptivity restricted to women and mares would support the claim; a documented case in any other species would refute the 'only' wording.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of mammalian reproductive behaviour, some of which note estrus or mating during pregnancy

obstacles: Mating during gestation is rarely a coded field, so the test is a compilation of narrative accounts.
Captive breeding logs that would settle doubtful species are mostly closed.
rationale: The behaviour is observable, and one well-documented species besides women and mares would refute the exclusive wording. Public natural-history accounts mention pregnancy and estrus, but they do not survey the behaviour systematically. The comparison can be started from those accounts and cannot be finished for mammals as a whole without further compilation.

operationalization: In pregnant hares, score whether one female carries embryos of two distinct developmental ages, or conceives again before the first litter is born. Repeated findings of two cohorts in Lepus would support superfetation; large samples of pregnant hares with only one embryonic stage would refute it for those species.
obstacles: The embryo-age counts are in species papers, not in a life-history database column.
The semen-richness and many-toes explanations are separate from the embryological finding.
rationale: Superfetation in hares has a direct anatomical criterion, and published dissections of European hares already report embryos of different ages. Those counts are enough to test the natural-history claim for Lepus and are not assembled as a downloadable dataset. The causal gloss that hares superfetate because they are small, many-toed and spermatic is not in those same counts.

operationalization: Using age at eye opening, treat birth with eyes open as fully formed and eye opening days after birth as imperfect. Compare solid-hoofed and cloven-hoofed ungulates with many-toed carnivores such as dog, wolf, fox, bear and lion. Eyes open at birth in the hoofed groups, and closed in most of the many-toed group, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: species-level age at eye opening, the direct measure of being born blind, for ungulates and fissiped carnivores

obstacles: Age at eye opening is missing for many species, though the genera Aristotle names are among the better filled.
The pig is cloven-hoofed and is the exception the surrounding text already flags, so it should be reported separately.
rationale: PanTHERIA includes age at eye opening, which matches Aristotle's imperfect young, many of them born blind. Hoof type maps cleanly onto perissodactyls, artiodactyls and fissiped carnivores. A table of that one variable for the named groups decides the contrast with standard comparative methods.

operationalization: Enucleate or destroy the eyes of nestling swallows and score, over subsequent weeks, whether a new eye forms and whether sight returns. Regrowth with restored sight would support the claim; healed orbits without a reformed eye would refute it.
obstacles: No public series records the outcome of eye removal in nestling swallows.
General descriptions of avian eye development are not a substitute for that injury series.
rationale: The prediction is experimentally crisp: either the nestling eye regrows after being put out, or it does not. No open dataset contains that trial. Developmental descriptions of intact bird embryos do not record regeneration after enucleation, so the claim stays testable and untested by existing public data.

operationalization: Compute the male-to-female ratio of congenital anomalies in human population registries, then compare that sex ratio with veterinary series for other species. A male excess limited to humans would support the claim; a male excess in other animals, or no human sex difference, would refute the matching clause.

candidate_datasets.name: EUROCAT
candidate_datasets.role: sex-specific prevalence of human congenital anomalies

obstacles: Comparable population registries for other animals are sparse, so the cross-species clause is the weak half.
The sex ratio differs by anomaly, so 'defective' has to be fixed as all registered anomalies or as a pre-set list.
rationale: Human registries record anomaly prevalence by sex, which is enough to test whether males are more often born with defects. The second clause, that other animals lack this male excess, has no matching open registry. The human half can be decided now and the comparative half cannot.

operationalization: Compare the sexes on fetal growth or gestational age at birth, age at puberty, and the age schedule of mortality. Females later on prenatal milestones and earlier at puberty would support those two clauses; the ageing clause needs a pre-chosen marker, such as age at menopause versus male reproductive senescence, before a result counts as confirmation or refutation.

candidate_datasets.name: INTERGROWTH-21st
candidate_datasets.role: fetal and newborn size standards by sex, for the prenatal half of the claim

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: postnatal growth by sex, as a bridge from birth to puberty

candidate_datasets.name: Human Mortality Database
candidate_datasets.role: sex-specific human mortality schedules for the timing of old age

obstacles: Male fetuses are often slightly larger, so 'develops more slowly' depends on which prenatal milestone is chosen.
Women have longer mean lifespans, so 'old age sooner' is not the same variable as age at death.
rationale: Open growth standards and national mortality schedules contain the sex differences in fetal size, childhood growth and lifespan. Puberty timing is also well measured, though it sits in demographic surveys rather than in these three files alone. 'Prime of life' and 'old age' still need an agreed marker, and that choice can change the verdict on the postnatal half, so the claim is only partly fixed as a test.

operationalization: Among women still breastfeeding, estimate the rates of resumed menses and of a new conception, and, where recorded, whether milk production stops after conception. Near-zero rates of menses and conception, and cessation of milk when conception occurs, would support the claim; substantial rates of either event, or continued lactation in pregnancy, would refute the absolute wording.

candidate_datasets.name: Demographic and Health Surveys
candidate_datasets.role: breastfeeding status, postpartum amenorrhea and birth intervals, from which conception during lactation can be estimated

obstacles: Surveys measure amenorrhea and birth intervals, and they do not record whether milk dries up after a new conception.
Lactational amenorrhea is common under specific conditions, so the absolute wording and the tendency need to be scored separately.
rationale: Demographic and Health Surveys record breastfeeding, the return of menses and the spacing of the next birth for large samples of women. Those variables decide whether nursing women 'do not' menstruate or conceive, once 'do not' is read as a rate near zero. They do not record milk supply after a conception during lactation, so that clause remains outside the open survey files.

operationalization: Record the usual presentation at spontaneous birth: head-first versus breech or tail-first. A large majority of head-first births in humans and in other viviparous mammals would support a general tendency; a species whose ordinary delivery is tail-first or breech would refute the claim that every animal is born head-first.

candidate_datasets.name: NBER Vital Statistics Natality Birth Data
candidate_datasets.role: US births with fetal presentation, for the human case

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts that describe birth presentation in other mammals, including aquatic species

obstacles: Presentation is a coded field for human births and only a scattered remark for other mammals.
'Natural' birth sets aside obstructed labours, which has to be defined before breech counts are interpreted.
rationale: Human natality files code cephalic versus breech presentation at population scale. For other viviparous animals the same fact is in narrative accounts and veterinary papers, including tail-first birth in whales, and those accounts are not a trait table. The universal claim can be dented by well-described exceptions and cannot be surveyed across mammals from one file.

operationalization: Rank species by recorded maximum longevity and see whether humans exceed every species except elephants. Any species with a credible maximum above the human record, other than elephants, would refute the claim; humans above all species except elephants would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: curated maximum longevity for humans, elephants and other animals

obstacles: Maximum-longevity records favour captive and well-studied species.
The restated claim uses modern credible evidence, which is wider than the animals Aristotle had seen.
rationale: AnAge is a curated, downloadable table of maximum longevity built for this comparison. Humans, both elephant species and longer-lived vertebrates are in it, so the ranking can be read off directly. Sampling bias affects the least-studied species and does not prevent a clear test against the animals with the best records.

operationalization: In viviparous mammals, compare phylogenetic regressions of gestation length on neonate mass and on maximum longevity, each controlling adult body mass. A stronger partial association with offspring size than with lifespan would support the claim; a stronger association with lifespan, once size is held constant, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length, neonate mass, adult mass and maximum longevity for mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: independently curated gestation and longevity for the same comparison

obstacles: Adult size, offspring size, gestation and lifespan move together, so partial correlations remain confounded.
A closer correlation with offspring size is evidence about prediction, and the tables do not identify a cause.
rationale: The three variables Aristotle contrasts are in open mammal life-history tables, and a phylogenetic partial regression is a standard analysis. That analysis can show whether gestation tracks offspring size more closely than lifespan. It cannot isolate 'the real cause', because size sits underneath all of the correlations, so the mechanistic wording stays only partly tested.

operationalization: Compare measured gestation means for horses, humans and elephants with one year, ten months and two years, stating in advance whether a month is lunar or calendar and what tolerance counts as agreement. Means inside that tolerance support the stated durations; means outside it refute them.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for horse, human and both living elephant species

obstacles: Ten months is about 295 days if the months are lunar and about 304 if they are calendar months, so the human comparison needs that choice fixed first.
Horse and elephant gestations have ranges, and the claim states a single duration.
rationale: Gestation length for Equus caballus, Homo sapiens, Elephas maximus and Loxodonta africana is a standard field in AnAge. The comparison is a lookup once the ancient month-length is fixed. The numbers are specific enough that the data can confirm or refute each stated duration within a declared tolerance.

operationalization: The claim sorts variable traits, such as an individual's eye colour, into final causation versus material and efficient necessity. No measurement of colour, frequency or fitness distinguishes those causal kinds once the colour itself is granted.
obstacles: Final cause and material necessity predict the same observed eye colours.
rationale: Iris colour is measurable, and the claim is about which kind of cause it has when it is not fixed for the whole kind. Any observed colour, and any selective advantage or lack of one, can be described either as for a purpose or as a material consequence. Nothing in existing data separates those descriptions.

operationalization: Score fetal behavioural states, or movement bouts, as a fraction of observed time in late pregnancy, and the same fraction in newborns. A large majority of time in quiet states, interrupted by brief active periods, would support the claim; predominantly active fetuses, or no active periods before birth, would refute the matching clause.
obstacles: Calling a fetal quiet state 'sleep' depends on a behavioural definition that EEG studies apply mainly to sheep.
Open series are human ultrasound cohorts, while the claim also cites oviparous embryos.
rationale: Human fetal-behaviour studies and a smaller experimental literature on other species already time quiet and active periods before birth. Those series are papers, not a shared archive, and they cover humans far better than animal embryos generally. The time budget can be compiled for late human fetuses and newborns, with a standing dispute about whether the quiet state is sleep.

operationalization: In video of infants of a pre-set age, code laughter and crying during scored wake and sleep. Laughter and crying confined to sleep, with no waking laughter, would support the claim; any reliable waking laughter in that age window would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Databrary
candidate_datasets.role: research video of human infants, with behavioural coding that can include sleep, wake, smiling and crying

obstacles: Databrary access is restricted, and laughter is not a field already extracted for every volume.
The result depends on whether 'infants' means newborns or babies old enough for social laughter.
rationale: Wake versus sleep and laughter versus crying are codable events, and infant video libraries hold the raw material. Access restrictions and the age definition mean a full test is a coding project on a subset of volumes, not a query of a finished table. Published coding studies already speak to neonatal smiles in sleep and to later waking laughter, which is why the claim is partly testable now.

operationalization: Record iris colour at birth and again in later infancy, stratified by ancestry, and note whether other mammals show a similar shift. Newborns with dark irises that stay dark would refute 'all children'; a human shift that is also obvious in another species would refute the comparative clause.
obstacles: No open longitudinal file links iris colour at birth to later colour across ancestries.
Neonatal eye colour in other animals is in veterinary notes rather than a trait table.
rationale: Birth colour and later colour are ordinary clinical observations, and a dark-eyed newborn population would refute the universal. The relevant series are published pediatric samples, uneven across ancestries, and there is no open dataset that follows the same children. Animal comparisons are thinner still, so both clauses can be probed from the literature and neither is in a downloadable cohort.

operationalization: List species with stable within-species iris-colour classes and species with heterochromia, and rank horses against humans and other mammals. Heterochromia, or several iris colours, in a species other than horses and humans would refute the exclusive clause; a wider palette in horses than in other non-human mammals would support the variety clause.

candidate_datasets.name: OMIA: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: inherited heterochromia and iris-pigmentation phenes in dogs, pigs, cattle, sheep, horses, cats and other domestic species

obstacles: OMIA records genetic cases, not a census of how many iris colours each species has.
Wild mammals are largely absent, so 'no other animal' is tested mainly among domestic species.
rationale: OMIA documents heterochromia in several mammals besides the horse, which is enough to test the claim that the two-coloured eye is seen in no other animal. It does not rank species by the number of ordinary iris colours, so 'the greatest variety' is only partly covered. Domestic species are the well-catalogued slice; the rest of the animal kingdom is not.

operationalization: Compare photopic acuity or contrast sensitivity, and a scotopic test, across people grouped by measured iris colour, controlling age, refractive error and ancestry. Worse daytime scores in blue-eyed groups and worse nighttime scores in dark-eyed groups would support the claim; the opposite pattern, or no difference, would refute it.
obstacles: Open cohorts that measure acuity rarely also record iris colour and a separate night test.
Iris colour tracks ancestry and fundus pigmentation, which can mimic an effect of eye colour.
rationale: Daytime and nighttime visual performance by iris colour is a standard psychophysical comparison, and small clinical studies have measured pieces of it. No named open dataset holds iris colour together with matched photopic and scotopic scores. Existing papers allow a partial, confounded test, and a clean one would need variables that are not currently joined.

operationalization: Estimate cataract prevalence and night-blindness prevalence by iris colour, controlling age, ancestry, UV exposure and diabetes. Higher cataract rates in blue-eyed people and higher night-blindness rates in dark-eyed people would support the two clauses; reversed or null associations would refute them.

candidate_datasets.name: UK Biobank Showcase
candidate_datasets.role: self-reported cataract and age at cataract diagnosis in a large adult cohort; iris colour is not a showcase field, so the eye-colour split still has to come from elsewhere

obstacles: Night blindness has many causes and is poorly captured next to iris colour.
Iris colour is entangled with ancestry and lifetime UV exposure.
rationale: Cataract is common enough, and is recorded at scale in UK Biobank, that an association with iris colour is an ordinary epidemiological question. The showcase does not itself provide iris colour, and night blindness is a heterogeneous symptom spread across retinal diseases. Published studies can be compiled for a partial test of the cataract clause, with serious confounding, and they do not jointly decide both halves.

operationalization: Score orbital prominence, or corneal protrusion relative to the skull, and regress visual acuity on that score across species. Higher acuity in deep-set eyes, after controlling eye size and habitat, would support the claim; no relationship, or the reverse, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Ecological and morphological correlates of acuity in birds
candidate_datasets.role: avian visual acuity with eye size and habitat; orbital prominence is not a column and would have to be added

obstacles: The open acuity table uses eye size and ecology, which are not the same variable as a prominent versus deep-set eye.
Habitat and phylogeny can produce the same acuity differences Aristotle attributes to eye position.
rationale: Comparative acuity for dozens of bird species is downloadable, with eye size and habitat already attached. Prominence of the eye is a further morphological judgment and is absent from that table. Joining skull or photograph scores to the acuity file would test a proxy, and eye size plus ecology would still confound a claim specifically about how deeply the eye sits.

operationalization: Score presence or absence of an external pinna in earless seals, especially the Mediterranean monk seal, against sea lions and other aquatic mammals. Absence of a pinna and presence of an auditory opening in phocids would support the anatomical claim; a pinna in those seals would refute it. Pinnae in other aquatic mammals would count against the explanation that aquatic life itself removes the external ear.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: family and species accounts stating whether phocids, otariids and other aquatic mammals have external ear flaps

obstacles: Aristotle's seal is the monk seal, a phocid; sea lions have small pinnae and are a different family.
The accounts state the anatomy directly and do not measure the auditory canal.
rationale: Presence or absence of an external ear is unambiguous, and public species accounts record it for phocids and for the aquatic mammals that still have pinnae. That is enough to confirm or refute the anatomical claim for the seals Aristotle meant, and to test the further claim that life in the water is what removes the ear. The explanatory clause is weaker than the anatomy, because otariids and otters remain in the comparison.

operationalization: For humans, horses and a sample of other mammals, record whether hair or fur on the head turns grey with age. Greying common in humans, weaker in horses and absent elsewhere would support the claim; obvious age-greying in another mammal would refute the 'practically any other animal' clause.

candidate_datasets.name: OMIA: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: progressive greying of the horse, and any other catalogued species in which coat colour lightens with age

obstacles: OMIA records the horse greying mutation and does not survey wild mammals for age-related greying.
Dogs and some primates are the likely rival cases, and they are described in papers rather than a trait column.
rationale: Human greying and the progressive greying syndrome of horses are both well described, and OMIA records the horse trait as a genetic phene. A systematic check of other mammals is not in that catalogue. The horse clause and the existence of human greying can be confirmed from existing sources, while 'no other animal' requires a survey that has not been assembled.

operationalization: In adult men, code where baldness begins (frontal hairline, temples, crown, occiput) and where greying is first noticed. Baldness concentrated on the front, with no one bald first at the temples or the back, and greying beginning at the temples, would support the claim; a common temporal or occipital onset of baldness would refute that clause.

candidate_datasets.name: UK Biobank Showcase
candidate_datasets.role: male self-reported hair/balding pattern for more than 200,000 men, distinguishing frontal and crown patterns

obstacles: The balding item does not record where greying starts.
Patterns are self-reported in a cohort that is mostly of European ancestry.
rationale: UK Biobank asks men which balding pattern they have, in categories that separate a frontal pattern from crown involvement, so the baldness-location clause can be tested at once. The same resource does not ask where hair turns grey first. Temple-first greying remains in clinical description rather than in that table, so only half of the sentence is in the open cohort.

operationalization: Score hair form (straight, wavy, curly) for populations in cold moist and hot dry climates, then test the association after accounting for ancestry. Straight hair in the cold moist group and curly hair in the hot group, with the association surviving an ancestry control, would support the geographic clause; a null residual association would count against climate as the cause.

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: temperature and precipitation surfaces for the regions named in the claim

candidate_datasets.name: ALFRED
candidate_datasets.role: population allele frequencies, including variants associated with hair form, as a proxy for the phenotype

obstacles: Hair form tracks ancestry, so a climate correlation can be population history.
Scythians and Thracians are ancient groups, and allele frequencies are a proxy for measured hair.
rationale: Climate surfaces for the Black Sea, Thrace and tropical Africa are public, and allele-frequency tables include loci associated with hair shape. Direct hair-form measurements for the peoples Aristotle names are not in those files. Even a modern correlation of curl with temperature would leave ancestry as a serious confound, so the test can be sketched and cannot cleanly separate climate from descent.

operationalization: For echinoids with a known depth, compare spine length and test diameter between shallow sites and sites at or below about 110 metres, and attach local temperature where it exists. Small tests with disproportionately long, robust spines in the deep cold sample would support the claim; no depth trend, or a trend that disappears within a single family, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: echinoid occurrences with depth, to separate deep from shallow records

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic backbone mapping sea-urchins to Echinoidea and to families with different spine types

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: species summaries of depth and habitat; numeric spine length still has to be compiled from descriptions

obstacles: Aristotle's deep-water urchin is not identified to a modern species.
Long spines are a family-level trait of cidaroids, so depth and phylogeny are confounded.
Deep Mediterranean water is not uniformly cold at sixty fathoms.
rationale: Occurrence databases place echinoids by depth, and taxonomic registers separate the families whose spines differ. Spine length and test diameter are in species descriptions rather than in those occurrence files. A depth comparison can be assembled for a subset of taxa, and it will not cleanly separate cold, depth and phylogeny.

operationalization: Compare the prevalence of male-pattern baldness in intact men, women and men castrated before or after puberty. Near-zero prevalence in women and in early-castrated men, against a high male prevalence, would support the claim; substantial male-pattern baldness in women or in early eunuchs would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: UK Biobank Showcase
candidate_datasets.role: male balding-pattern frequencies, the contrast class; the item was not asked of women

obstacles: The open balding question covers men, so women and eunuchs are outside it.
Eunuch evidence is a small set of clinical series, and female-pattern hair loss is a different phenotype.
rationale: Male balding prevalence is measurable in a large open cohort, which fixes the background rate the claim contrasts with women and eunuchs. Women were not asked that question, and castrated men are not identified in it. The sex difference and the effect of early castration are described in dermatology series that can be compiled, and they are not one public table.

operationalization: Compare age at first greying, or the proportion of grey hair at a fixed age, between people who habitually cover the scalp and people who do not, controlling ancestry and dye use. Earlier greying in the covered group would support the claim; no difference, or later greying, would refute it.
obstacles: No open cohort records head-covering habit together with age at greying.
Sun exposure, genetics and hair treatments would confound a future comparison.
rationale: The prediction is a difference in greying age by whether the hair is kept covered. Public cohorts record neither hat use nor the onset of greying as a pair. The comparison is feasible as a new study and is not sitting in existing files.

operationalization: Search identified photographs of partridges, ravens, sparrows and bears for individuals that are white or largely white while the species is ordinarily dark. One well-documented white individual in each named group would support the existence claim; a thorough search with none in a group would leave that group unsupported.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: identified photographs of partridges, ravens, sparrows and bears that can be scored for white plumage or pelage

obstacles: Unusual animals are photographed more often, which inflates apparent frequency and does not block an existence test.
'Partridge' and 'sparrow' cover several genera, and the white-phase black bear is a colour morph rather than albinism.
rationale: The claim is that white individuals have been observed in otherwise uniform kinds, which is an existence test. Identified public photographs of the four groups can be scored for white plumage or pelage in a short review. Frequency would be biased by what people choose to photograph; occurrence of the white individuals would not.

operationalization: Within a many-coloured domestic species, relate coat colour to the temperature of the water the animals drink, holding breed constant. Whiter coats on hot water and darker coats on cold water would support the claim; no association would refute it.
obstacles: Drinking-water temperature is not recorded with coat colour.
Breed, minerals and sunlight would confound any regional comparison.
rationale: The mechanism predicts a within-species colour change caused by the temperature of drinking water. Coat-colour records and water-temperature records are not joined in any public file, and coat colour is largely genetic. The experiment is conceivable and the paired data are absent.

operationalization: For a sample of species that are not a single colour, measure dorsal and ventral luminance on standardised images. A lighter underside in all, or nearly all, such species would support the claim; a substantial set of non-uniform species with a darker belly would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographs of patterned animals that can be scored for a lighter underside

obstacles: Lighting and camera angle bias any luminance read from field photographs.
Ventral colour is not a pre-coded column, so the test is a scoring project.
rationale: A lighter belly on patterned animals is a luminance comparison, and public photograph archives contain the animals. The colour is in the pixels rather than in a trait field, and field lighting makes the measurement noisy. A scored subset can test the tendency, and it will not cleanly cover 'all animals'.

operationalization: Measure fundamental frequency of sexed recordings and test whether females are higher than males, with cattle as a pre-specified exception. A female advantage in most sampled species, a large human difference, and a lower female pitch in cattle would support the claim; a male advantage in many species, or cows higher than bulls, would refute the matching clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Xeno-canto
candidate_datasets.role: sex-annotated bird recordings from which fundamental frequency can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: sex-annotated vertebrate recordings, including mammals, for the same comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Mozilla Common Voice
candidate_datasets.role: sex-labelled human speech for the species in which the claim says the difference is greatest

obstacles: Sex labels are incomplete, and cattle calls with known sex are scarce in wildlife archives.
Pitch must be fundamental frequency; loudness and repertoire size are different variables.
rationale: Open sound archives label sex for many birds and some mammals, and a speech corpus does the same for humans, so fundamental frequency by sex is a standard measurement. Coverage is good for birds and humans and thin for cattle, which is the stated exception. The general and human clauses can be tested on existing recordings; the cattle reversal needs a separate, smaller set of sexed calls.

operationalization: Dissect or image a series of bull hearts and record whether a bone (os cordis) is present. Any positive cases would support 'some bulls'; a large series with none would refute the claim for the cattle examined.
obstacles: Prevalence counts are in veterinary anatomy papers and are not deposited as a dataset.
The bone is also reported in cows, which the wording 'some bulls' does not rule out.
rationale: Presence of a cardiac bone is a yes-or-no anatomical finding, and published cattle dissections already report it in some animals. Those series are small, scattered and not an open file of specimens. They are enough to test the existence claim for Bos taurus and are short of a downloadable prevalence table.

operationalization: Compare fundamental frequency, and a pre-chosen set of sex-typical behaviours, before and after castration or between castrated and intact males of the same species. A shift toward the female pitch and toward the female behavioural scores in every sampled species would support the claim; species with no voice change, or a change away from the female pattern, would refute the universal.
obstacles: Sound archives do not label geldings, steers or castrati as a class.
'Female character' has no single variable, and the effect depends on whether castration is before or after puberty.
rationale: Voice pitch after castration is measured in studies of castrati, geldings and steers, and those studies are papers rather than a cross-species archive. 'Character' adds temperament and behaviour, which are only loosely operational. The voice clause can be compiled for a few domestic species and humans, and 'all animals' remains far beyond the samples.

operationalization: From dental eruption schedules, record which deciduous teeth are shed and replaced in the pig and in the lion. No replacement in the pig, and replacement limited to the canines in the lion, would support the claim; replacement of incisors or premolars in either species would refute the corresponding clause.
obstacles: Eruption schedules for pig and lion are in veterinary references, not in one comparative download.
The claim's 'some carnivores' is illustrated by the lion, so other carnivores should be reported as a separate check.
rationale: Tooth replacement is a standard veterinary schedule for the domestic pig and a published schedule for the lion, and either schedule can confirm or refute the clause about that species. The tables are short and public in the literature, and they are not a single open dataset. A small compilation decides the two named animals; it does not automatically extend to every carnivore.

operationalization: The principle says nature never fails and does nothing in vain, so far as is possible in each case. Any apparent failure can be set aside as impossible in that case, so no observation distinguishes the principle from its denial.
obstacles: The saving clause 'so far as is possible in each case' absorbs counterexamples.
Vestiges, disease and developmental error are compatible with the principle under that clause.
rationale: The sentence is a standing assumption about nature's purposes, qualified so that whatever occurs was possible and whatever does not occur was not. Anatomical and life-history datasets describe what organisms do. They do not supply a result that would confirm the principle against a rival that allows nature to fail or to act without a purpose.

operationalization: Within a suckling species, relate milk temperature at feeding to the age at which the teeth erupt, holding litter size and body mass constant. Earlier eruption on hotter milk would support the claim; no association would refute it.
obstacles: Milk temperature and age at tooth eruption are not stored together.
Cross-species differences in both variables follow body size and phylogeny.
rationale: The claim predicts that hotter milk advances the cutting of the teeth, which is a within-species association. Life-history tables have weaning age and sometimes eruption notes, and they do not have the temperature of the milk. The paired observations would have to be collected.

operationalization: From dental exams, estimate the proportion of people with a visible third molar by year of age, especially through the late teens and the twenties. A sharp rise centred near age twenty would support the main clause; a rise centred far from twenty would refute it. Eruption in old age has to be separated from late recognition of a tooth that erupted earlier.

candidate_datasets.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: oral-examination files that record whether each third molar is visible, by age

obstacles: A missing third molar may have been extracted or may still be impacted, so absence is not a date of eruption.
Some survey cycles do not examine adults in their twenties, and eruption in old age is not timed.
rationale: NHANES dentition exams record visible third molars across age, which is a usable proxy for whether the last grinders have cut the gum by about twenty. Extraction and impaction mean the age curve is not a pure eruption schedule, and the exams do not date a tooth that appears in old age. The central age claim can be bounded from these files, and the late-life clause cannot.
